ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a vertically placed cylindrical barrel, which can rotate around the vertical axis in the middle; the dashed line represents the central axis, and there is a curved arrow above indicating rotation. Near the center of the upper surface of the cylindrical barrel, a black dot is drawn, and a thin string goes obliquely downward from this point to the block near the inner wall on the left side; the block is against the inner wall of the cylindrical barrel. The string makes a certain angle with the vertical direction, which can be denoted as θ. Reasoning: The block undergoes uniform circular motion together with the cylindrical barrel, and there is no acceleration in the vertical direction. Since the inner wall of the cylindrical barrel is smooth, the barrel wall has only a horizontal support force on the block and cannot provide vertical friction. The block is acted on by gravity mg downward, string tension T along the string pointing toward the center of the upper surface, and the support force N of the barrel wall horizontally pointing toward the center. In the vertical direction it is in equilibrium, so T cosθ = mg. The block is always against the inner wall of the cylindrical barrel, and the string length and the radius of the cylindrical barrel determine its geometric position; therefore θ does not change as the angular velocity increases, so T = mg/cosθ is a constant. When the angular velocity increases, the required centripetal force increases, which is mainly manifested as a change in the horizontal support force N, rather than a change in the string tension. Final answer: As the angular velocity of rotation increases, the tension in the string remains unchanged.
